title: AI Change Management and Team Integration

questions.question: Why is AI adoption not finished when a tool is available?
options: Because early adopters need time before the rest of the team can be given access
Because roles, handoffs, review duties, and behavior changes still need to be clear
Because the tool must pass a security review before anyone is allowed to open it
Because licence costs only become visible once the whole department is onboarded
questions.explanation: AI adoption requires operating routines and role clarity, not only tool access. Adoption stalls when teams cannot see who is accountable or when AI use is allowed.

questions.question: Adoption of a new AI workflow stalled after the pilot. What does every such workflow still need?
options: A communication campaign, an internal launch event, and a short recorded demo per team
A dedicated budget line, a vendor support contract, and a named technical administrator
A role map, an explicit human review point, an adoption metric, and a way to handle exceptions
A model evaluation report, a latency benchmark, and a documented fallback to the older model
questions.explanation: The lesson defines team integration as four concrete pieces: a role map, an explicit human review point, an adoption metric, and exception handling. Communication alone does not close the gap, because AI change is a workflow redesign problem.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A change-readiness plan with priority, controls, and rationale
A reorganisation chart that assigns each person a new reporting line
A training curriculum generated automatically from each employee's role
A compliance attestation that clears the rollout for the whole department
questions.explanation: The artifact scores adoption signals and returns priority, controls, and rationale, so team integration decisions can be compared rather than argued.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: A tool ban that blocks AI use until the governance policy is finalised
A role map that states who does what in the changed workflow and who reviews it
An anonymous usage log that hides which team produced which output
A one-off launch email that announces the tool and closes the rollout
questions.explanation: A role map clarifies responsibilities around the changed workflow, including who reviews AI output. The lesson insists that human review points be explicit.

questions.question: When should rollout require stronger controls?
options: Only when the user interface has many screens and takes time to learn
Only when the tool has no active users left after the pilot has ended
Only when the vendor changes its pricing model partway through the year
When role impact, adoption friction, and governance uncertainty are high
questions.explanation: High adoption and governance risk require stronger rollout controls. Interface complexity and vendor pricing are not the signals this lesson scores.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the integration plan?
options: To translate AI adoption into team routines, owners, metrics, and controls
To replace the manager's role in deciding how the team allocates its work
To retire the training path once the first group of users is comfortable
To keep handoff problems out of the rollout review so momentum is kept
questions.explanation: The plan connects change management to concrete operating behavior, translating governance language into routines a team can actually follow.
